planting.note: Set out own-root container plants in spring into loamy, well-drained soil amended with compost; this low groundcover rose roots on its own crown so suckers stay true to type.

directions: This Patent #33,585 selection carries lightly fragrant red double blooms in continuous waves from spring through fall over a naturally rounded, groundcover-like frame. Grow it in enriched, well-drained soil and water once the top few inches dry out rather than on a fixed schedule. Cut the whole plant back by about a third each late winter to keep flowering wood renewed, and expect it to largely clean up its own spent petals. Its disease resistance makes it a reasonable no-spray choice for mixed borders, mass plantings, or large containers.

planting.note: Divide or transplant in spring into fertile, free-draining soil; this compact coneflower fills in quickly and rewards deep watering during its first season while roots establish.

directions: Patent #31,029 Fiesta opens coral-pink and softens in tone as each flower ages, so a single clump shows several hues at once from late spring into fall. It stays notably compact and self-branching compared with older coneflower strains, which keeps it from flopping in beds or mixed containers without staking. Deadhead spent blooms through summer to push out fresh flushes, and shear the clump back in early spring before new growth emerges. Once rooted in, it shrugs off dry spells and draws steady pollinator and bird traffic.

planting.note: Plant after frost risk has passed into enriched, slightly acidic, well-drained soil, or keep container-grown and bring indoors before temperatures drop; this tropical hibiscus needs steady warmth to perform.

directions: Patent #34,663 Gold produces oversized golden-yellow blooms with a deep red throat set against glossy, dark green leaves through the warm months. Keep soil consistently moist rather than letting it dry between waterings, and feed lightly just before spring growth resumes to fuel the long bloom run. Prune after flowering tapers off to maintain a tidy, formal shape and encourage branching. In cooler zones, grow it in a pot so it can be moved under cover before frost, since it has no cold hardiness to speak of.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine fines; this ornamental selection earns its spot in a border as much for foliage color as for fruit.

directions: Belle's new growth emerges an unusual icy rose shade on pink stems before settling into green, giving this plant ornamental value well beyond its early-season crop of large, plump berries. It needs roughly 800 hours of winter chill to fruit well, so it suits moderate-winter climates rather than mild coastal gardens. Keep the root zone moist but never soggy, and give it afternoon shade where summers run hot to protect foliage color. Light pruning after harvest is enough to keep the habit shapely.

common_name: Chateau de Saumur Rose of Sharon

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in spring into well-drained soil; this vase-shaped selection tolerates coastal salt exposure, making it a good choice near walkways and drives as well as open borders.

directions: De Saumur is the first double-flowered member of the Chateau series, opening frilly, violet-pink blooms along the full length of each stem rather than only at the branch tips, so the whole shrub reads as colorful rather than just its top edge. It blooms from early summer through fall and holds up to hummingbird and pollinator traffic without excessive deadheading. Water deeply through the first season to establish a deep root system, after which it tolerates short dry spells. Prune right after flowering if you want to control size or encourage denser rebloom next year.

planting.note: Move outdoors after nights stay reliably above 45F into humusy, well-drained soil in a sheltered, shaded spot; this Dan Hinkley collection begonia is grown for its oversized leaves as much as for its flowers.

directions: Caldera's massive, glossy, heart-shaped leaves emerge deep red and unfurl to bright green, giving it the presence of a specimen foliage plant even before the nodding white spring flowers and round seed pods appear. It wants humid air and protection from direct midday sun, so a shaded patio or understory planting suits it better than open exposure. Let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings rather than keeping it saturated. Where winters drop below about 45F, grow it in a container and bring it indoors rather than leaving it to face frost.

planting.note: Plant in spring into enriched, consistently moist, well-drained soil with a layer of mulch; this compact mophead holds up to sun and heat better than older varieties thanks to thicker, waxier leaves.

directions: Hanalei Bay's slightly frilled mophead blooms open deep magenta with a light green to white center and keep repeating from spring through summer on a compact, rounded frame. Its thicker, waxier foliage resists the wilting and scorch that undermine older hydrangeas during hot afternoons, but it still performs best with some shade and should never be allowed to dry out fully. Feed in early spring as new growth begins, and deadhead spent flower heads along with any weak stems through the season. It fits well in foundation plantings or large containers where its reblooming habit extends color longer than a one-shot variety.
